clue.text: Something shiny in church where the Pope is

blocks.note: The Pope lives in the Vatican, in the Italian capital

explanation.surface: Someone spots a glittering object in the Pope's own church.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'in church where the Pope is' as one place, but 'in' is only a link and the church and the Pope's city are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Chrome is chromium plating, the bright polished metal trim seen on cars and taps.

clue.text: Merciful post-war PM

blocks.note: An adjective for someone who shows leniency
The Labour prime minister elected in 1945 after the Second World War

explanation.walkthrough: Clement Attlee was the British prime minister from 1945 to 1951, succeeding Churchill.
explanation.definitionFit: As an ordinary adjective the word means lenient or showing mercy, and it was also Attlee's first name.

clue.text: Set aside area of responsibility

blocks.note: A verb: to cancel or waive a penalty or debt
A noun: the scope of a person's or body's duties

explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs the two meanings together as a single phrase; split after 'aside' to find a verb and a noun sharing one spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means cancel or waive a punishment; as a noun it is the brief or scope given to a committee.

clue.text: Arts graduate about to join little woman in play

blocks.note: Circa, the Latin for about, abbreviated
One of the four March sisters in Alcott's novel Little Women

explanation.surface: A graduate is about to be cast alongside a small actress in a stage production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little woman' is not a short woman but a character from Little Women: Beth March.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy about the Scottish king is one of the most famous stage dramas ever written.

clue.text: Stress bill will need a bit of money added

blocks.note: Short for account, a bill to be paid
A small coin, one hundredth of a dollar or euro

explanation.surface: A worrying bill arrives, with a small extra charge tacked on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stress' looks like worry to match the bill, but it is the emphasis on a syllable; AC is the usual shorthand for account.
explanation.definitionFit: In speech an accent is the emphasis placed on a particular syllable, just like stress.

clue.text: Squat in Essex river

blocks.note: A verb for bending low on one's heels
A river in the English county of Essex, whose estuary is popular with sailors

explanation.surface: Someone is squatting, perhaps illegally occupying a building, somewhere in Essex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squat in' suggests occupying a property; Essex is a county east of London and the River Crouch runs through it.
explanation.definitionFit: To crouch is to bend the knees and lower the body close to the ground, as in a squat.

clue.text: Preacher no longer one who thumps

explanation.surface: A preacher who used to bang the pulpit has given up the habit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a retired pulpit-thumper, but 'no longer' just supplies a prefix and the thumper supplies the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who expounds explains and sets out doctrine at length, which is what a preacher does in a sermon.

clue.text: Aunt is rambling around one African country

indicators.note: The mixed letters go around 'one', enclosing it

explanation.surface: A garrulous aunt goes on and on about some country in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange the letters of 'Aunt is' into TUNISA, then drop I in between TUNIS and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunisia is a North African nation on the Mediterranean coast, between Algeria and Libya.

clue.text: Teachers sorting out the classrooms

indicators.note: Sorting out rearranges things into a new order, as these letters must be

explanation.surface: Staff are tidying up their rooms at the start of term.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder sits squarely in the answer's own world, which makes the anagram easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: The old-fashioned term for male teachers at a school, now mostly replaced by gender-neutral words.

clue.text: Broadcast making one smile

blocks.note: A verb: to transmit a signal or programme

explanation.surface: A cheerful programme on the radio puts a grin on a listener's face.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Broadcast' a noun that causes a smile, but both halves are verbs defining the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: To beam a signal is to transmit it; to beam is also to give a wide, radiant grin.

clue.text: Plant needs crazy amount of liquid

blocks.note: An imperial measure, a pint of beer or milk

explanation.surface: A potted plant is being drowned by an owner who waters it far too much.
explanation.walkthrough: Cuckoo pint is a British wildflower, also called lords-and-ladies, little known outside Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuckoo pint is the wild arum, a woodland species with a hooded spathe and bright red berries.

clue.text: Understand article and be furious

blocks.note: As in 'I see what you mean'

explanation.surface: Someone reads a newspaper piece, grasps its meaning and is enraged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper piece, but here it is the grammatical word.
explanation.definitionFit: To seethe is to boil inwardly with rage, a vivid verb for being very angry.

clue.text: Old female leads the way, naturally

explanation.surface: An elderly woman shows everyone where to go, as you would expect.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Old female' as a person, but she splits into two single-letter abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are adverbial ways of saying something is obvious or to be expected.

clue.text: Talk and smooch freely, when abandoning a city

indicators.note: Abandoning means leaving behind, so 'a' is dropped from the letters

blocks.note: The letter removed from the combined fodder

explanation.surface: Two lovers chat and kiss openly as they leave a town behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Take TALK and SMOOCH together, remove one A, and rearrange the remaining nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockholm is the capital of Sweden, a large Scandinavian city spread across islands.

clue.text: Chap comes out with those unfair comments

definitions.note: The answer is singular; the clue's definition is plural

indicators.note: Things that come out emerge in a new form

explanation.surface: A man emerges and makes some snide remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes out with' looks like 'says', but 'with' is the link and the man and 'those' are the letters to mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheap shot is a mean, unsporting remark aimed at an easy target.

clue.text: Guide always offers this thought

blocks.note: Runs across the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A tour guide always has a suggestion to share.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans 'guIDE Always'.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea is a notion or concept formed in the mind, a direct synonym for a thought.

clue.text: It's absolutely right to get together

blocks.note: An archaic adjective for fitting or proper, as in old prayer-book language about what is right and just
A verb for coming together with someone

explanation.surface: Someone insists a reunion is exactly the right thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: The old adjective survives in the Anglican prayer book phrase 'it is meet and right so to do'.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic adjective means suitable or proper, while the verb means assemble or encounter.

clue.text: Extremities of planet full of spirit

explanation.surface: The far ends of some world are brimming with an ethereal essence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' suggests something ghostly, but in crosswords it is usually a strong drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Margins are the outer edges or borders of something, its furthest limits.

clue.text: Come down with sombre nobleman

blocks.note: As an aircraft or bird comes to earth

explanation.surface: Someone falls ill alongside a gloomy aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come down with' suggests catching an illness, but 'with' only joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A landgrave was a German count with jurisdiction over a territory, a title of high rank.

clue.text: Man climbing trail — before he makes this?

definitions.text: Man climbing trail — before he makes this?

indicators.note: In a down clue, climbing means reading upwards

blocks.note: The track or smell left by a quarry

explanation.surface: A mountaineer on the path up will, sooner or later, have to come back down.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: a man climbing a trail must at some point make the way down. ED reverses because the clue is a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A descent is a downward climb, what every climber must make after reaching the top.

clue.text: Seductress with anger — an evil character

blocks.note: A woman who uses her charm to exploit men

explanation.surface: A femme fatale in a rage turns out to be the villain of the story.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads the seductress as the evil character, and she is the first half of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A vampire is a blood-sucking undead monster of folklore, a classic villain in horror fiction.

clue.text: Second successful person, not the first, is a baddie

explanation.surface: The runner-up, rather than the champion, turns out to be the villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' reads like a runner-up, but it is just the abbreviation S.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinner is a wrongdoer who transgresses moral law, a plainly bad person.

clue.text: Strange artist keeping very quiet? I'm even quieter!

indicators.note: Something strange is out of its usual shape

blocks.note: Pianissimo, the musical marking for very soft

explanation.surface: An odd painter who barely speaks is outdone by someone quieter still.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks as the answer: a Trappist monk keeps silence, quieter even than PP.
explanation.definitionFit: Trappists are Cistercian monks famous for a strict rule of silence, hence even quieter than pianissimo.

clue.text: Sergeant major facing soldiers? One's unlikely to be this!

definitions.text: Sergeant major facing soldiers? One's unlikely to be this!

explanation.surface: A sergeant major confronting the troops is hardly going to be ingratiating.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines by contrast: a bawling sergeant major is the opposite of oily and flattering.
explanation.definitionFit: Smarmy means unctuously ingratiating, the last manner expected of a drill instructor shouting at recruits.

clue.text: Old Greek author sees river water rising

indicators.note: In a down clue, rising means reading upwards

blocks.note: The Italian river, a crossword favourite
A large body of salt water

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek writer watches the tide come up a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water rising' suggests a flood, but 'rising' reverses both river and water together.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek storyteller credited with the fables such as the tortoise and the hare.

clue.text: One may be in the dark when it comes to looking after people

definitions.text: One may be in the dark when it comes to looking after people

blocks.clueFragment: One may be in the dark
blocks.note: Surface reading: someone who is ignorant or uninformed

blocks.clueFragment: in the dark when it comes to looking after people
blocks.note: Setter's reading: someone literally working after nightfall caring for patients

explanation.surface: Someone is clueless about how to care for others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the dark' means ignorant in the surface, but literally it means working during night hours.
explanation.definitionFit: This hospital worker cares for patients on the overnight shift, literally in darkness.

clue.text: Son needs help, it's stated

explanation.surface: A boy requires assistance, so someone has declared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's stated' reads as a comment on the claim, but 'stated' is the definition and 'it's' only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Said is the past participle of say, meaning declared or expressed in words.

clue.text: With mockery a rite's made to look silly

indicators.note: Something made to look silly is knocked out of its proper form

blocks.note: Letters to be rearranged, with the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A solemn ceremony is lampooned and made ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator doubles as a gloss on the definition, so the surface nearly describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Satire is humour or ridicule used to expose folly, a form of derision or ridicule.

clue.text: Plain foot movement needed with gym

blocks.note: Physical education, the school gym lesson

explanation.surface: A simple dance move is required in the gym class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' reads as an adjective meaning simple, but it is the noun for flat grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: A steppe is a vast treeless grassland, as found across Russia and Central Asia.
